And he added: “The only thing remarked there was the absence of the clergy. No doubt the sacristies understand progress in a different way. As you please, gentlemen of Loyola!”

IX

Six weeks passed. Rodolphe did not return. One evening, at last, he appeared.

The day after the agricultural show, he had said to himself:

“Let us not go back too soon; that would be a mistake.”

And, at the end of the week, he had gone hunting. After the hunt, he had thought that it was too late; then he reasoned as follows:

“But if she loved me from the very first day, her impatience to see me again must make her love me more. So let us keep it up!”

And he realized that his calculation had been correct when, upon entering the room, he saw Emma turn pale.

She was alone. Daylight was fading. The little muslin curtains along the windowpanes deepened the twilight, and the gilding of the barometer, struck by a ray of sunlight, spread gleams in the mirror between the jagged outlines of the coral.

Rodolphe remained standing, and Emma barely answered his first polite remarks.

“As for me,” he said, “I had business to attend to. I was ill.”

“Seriously?” she cried.

“Well, no!” said Rodolphe, sitting down beside her on a stool. “The truth is, I did not want to come back.”

“Why?”

“Can’t you guess?”

He looked at her once more, but with such intensity that she lowered her head, blushing. He continued:

“Emma...”

“Sir!” she said, drawing slightly away.

“Ah! You see,” he replied in a melancholy voice, “that I was right to wish not to return; for that name, that name which fills my soul and which escaped my lips, you forbid me to use! Madame Bovary!... Why, everyone calls you that!... Besides, it is not your name; it is another man’s name!”

He repeated:

“Another man’s!”

And he hid his face in his hands.

“Yes, I think of you continually!... The memory of you drives me to despair! Ah, forgive me!... I shall leave you... Farewell!... I shall go far away..., so far that you will never hear of me again!... And yet..., today..., I do not know what force drove me toward you once more! For one does not struggle against heaven, one cannot resist the smile of angels! One lets oneself be carried away by what is beautiful, charming, adorable!”

It was the first time Emma had heard such things said to her; and her pride, like someone relaxing in a steam bath, stretched languidly and fully in the warmth of this language.

“But if I did not come,” he continued, “if I could not see you, ah! at least I gazed long upon everything around you. At night, every night, I would rise again, come as far as here, look at your house, the roof shining beneath the moon, the trees in the garden swaying by your window, and a little lamp, a gleam, shining through the panes in the darkness. Ah! Little did you know that there, so near and so far away, was a poor wretch...”

She turned toward him with a sob.

“Oh! You are kind!” she said.

“No, I love you, that is all! You do not doubt it! Tell me so; one word! Just one word!”

And Rodolphe, imperceptibly, let himself slide from the stool to the floor; but the clatter of wooden shoes was heard in the kitchen, and he noticed that the door to the room was not closed.

“How charitable it would be of you,” he continued, rising again, “to gratify a whim of mine!”

It was to visit her house; he wanted to become acquainted with it; and, Madame Bovary seeing no objection, they were both getting up when Charles came in.

“Good day, doctor,” Rodolphe said to him.

The physician, flattered by this unexpected title, poured forth obsequious courtesies, and the other man took advantage of them to recover his composure a little.

“Madame was speaking to me,” he then said, “about her health...”

Charles interrupted him: he did indeed have a thousand worries; his wife’s shortness of breath was returning. Rodolphe then asked whether horseback exercise might not be good for her.

“Certainly! Excellent, perfect!... There’s an idea! You ought to follow it.”

And when she objected that she had no horse, Monsieur Rodolphe offered her one; she declined his offer; he did not insist. Then, to provide a reason for his visit, he related that his carter, the man who had been bled, was still suffering from dizzy spells.

“I’ll stop by,” said Bovary.

“No, no, I’ll send him to you; we’ll come; that will be more convenient for you.”

“Ah! Very good. Thank you.”

And as soon as they were alone:

“Why don’t you accept Monsieur Boulanger’s proposals, which are so gracious?”

She put on a sulky expression, found a thousand excuses, and finally declared that perhaps it would look odd.

“Oh, I don’t care in the least!” said Charles, executing a pirouette. “Health before everything! You are wrong!”

“Oh! How do you expect me to ride when I have no riding habit?”

“You must order one!” he replied.

The riding habit decided her.

When the outfit was ready, Charles wrote to Monsieur Boulanger that his wife was at his disposal and that they were counting on his obligingness.

The next day at noon, Rodolphe arrived before Charles’s door with two saddle horses. One wore pink pom-poms on its ears and a ladies’ doeskin saddle.

Rodolphe had put on long, soft boots, telling himself that she had probably never seen any like them; and indeed Emma was delighted by his appearance when he came onto the landing in his long velvet coat and white knitted breeches. She was ready; she was waiting for him.

Justin slipped out of the pharmacy to see her, and the apothecary also left his work. He gave Monsieur Boulanger recommendations:

“An accident happens so quickly! Take care! Perhaps your horses are spirited!”

She heard a noise above her head: it was Félicité drumming on the windowpanes to amuse little Berthe. The child blew her a kiss from afar; her mother answered with a gesture made with the knob of her riding crop.

“Have a pleasant ride!” Monsieur Homais cried. “Be careful, above all! Be careful!”

And he waved his newspaper as he watched them ride away.
